content: Lung overdistension, also known as volutrauma, has been identified as a contributing factor in the development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) in neonates. Modern ventilation techniques for newborns include volume-targeted ventilation (VTV), which aims to deliver a consistent tidal volume, as opposed to traditional pressure-limited ventilation (PLV), which uses a fixed inflation pressure. The goal of VTV is to minimize lung injury and maintain stable levels of partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2). The objective of this study was to evaluate whether VTV, compared to PLV, reduces the rates of death or the combined outcome of death or BPD in neonates. Additionally, the study aimed to assess whether VTV influences other outcomes, such as air leaks, cranial ultrasound abnormalities, and neurodevelopmental progress. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal standard search strategy. Databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, covering studies up to January 13, 2017. Clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed. Investigators of included studies were contacted for additional information. The inclusion criteria were randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing VTV and PLV in infants younger than 44 weeks' postmenstrual age, with clinically relevant outcomes reported. The risk of bias in each trial was assessed using Cochrane methodology, and the quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using GRADE criteria. Data on mortality, BPD rates, short-term clinical outcomes, and long-term developmental outcomes were extracted. For categorical outcomes, risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and the number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) were calculated. For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MD) were estimated. A fixed-effect model was used for meta-analysis, and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported. A total of 20 randomized trials met the inclusion criteria, comprising 16 parallel trials with 977 infants and four cross-over trials with 88 infants. None of the studies were blinded, and the quality of evidence ranged from moderate to low. There was no significant difference in the primary outcome of death before hospital discharge between VTV and PLV modes (typical RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.07; low-quality evidence). However, moderate-quality evidence indicated that VTV reduced the combined outcome of death or BPD at 36 weeks' gestation (typical RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89; NNTB 8, 95% CI 5 to 20). VTV was also associated with reductions in several secondary outcomes. These included lower rates of pneumothorax (typical RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.87; NNTB 20, 95% CI 11 to 100), fewer mean days of mechanical ventilation (MD -1.35 days, 95% CI -1.83 to -0.86), reduced rates of hypocarbia (typical RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.72; NNTB 3, 95% CI 2 to 5), lower rates of severe intraventricular hemorrhage (grade 3 or 4) (typical RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.77; NNTB 11, 95% CI 7 to 25), and a reduction in the combined outcome of periventricular leukomalacia with or without severe intraventricular hemorrhage (typical RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.80; NNTB 11, 95% CI 7 to 33). Importantly, VTV was not associated with an increase in adverse outcomes. In conclusion, neonates ventilated with VTV had lower rates of death or BPD, pneumothorax, hypocarbia, severe cranial ultrasound abnormalities, and shorter durations of mechanical ventilation compared to those ventilated with PLV. Further research is necessary to determine whether VTV improves long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes and to optimize VTV strategies.
